closingStory: One of my favorite things about this shoot was that I could take the exact same studio environment and approach it in three completely different ways: clean and commercial, dark and monotone, and finally experimental and abstract. As for the editing, I kept each set fairly straightforward and edited the photographs according to what I wanted each one to feel like. The clean portraits stayed clean, the monotone set leaned into the dramatic black-and-white look, and the shutter-drag images were edited to emphasize the movement and abstraction rather than trying to make them look more conventional. Overall, I really enjoyed the Nikon Tour experience. I got to try a completely different camera system, learn something new, experiment with a technique I had only recently discovered, and make three very different kinds of photographs in the same shoot. And honestly, it left me thinking that maybe one day I really will own a camera from every major camera company. If I have the money for it, of course.

sections.text: I started seeing an ad for the Nikon Tour pop up on Instagram over and over again. This went on for a few days, and a couple of my photographer friends even asked me if I had heard about it and suggested that I should go. Eventually, I thought, you know what, why not?

The photographs you see here are from the Phoenix stop of the tour, which happened at Tempe Camera, right by ASU. Since I didn't have a vehicle at the time, I usually had to walk to places, and this was only about a 15-minute walk from where I used to live. I already knew Tempe Camera was an interesting place and, obviously, I love camera stores, so that was enough of a reason for me to go. One of my photographer friends also came along with me for the shoot.

There were different time slots available throughout the day, and I ended up going in the afternoon, pretty close to one of the last sessions of the day. It was also the final day of the Phoenix stop. The shoot itself was set up in a small studio in the basement of Tempe Camera, with two different sets. One was a simple white setup with flash, while the other had a much darker background with more dramatic lighting.

The whole idea behind the Nikon Tour was to let photographers actually get their hands on some of Nikon's newer cameras and try them out in a real shooting environment. You could test the cameras, experiment with different conditions, and get a feel for what they were like before deciding whether you wanted to buy one. There was even a special offer running during the tour, which definitely made the whole thing feel like a pretty good opportunity.

At the time, I wasn't really a Nikon shooter. I'd used a Nikon DSLR beforeit was actually one of the first cameras I ever usedbut I had moved over to Sony. It wasn't because I was loyal to one particular brand. Switching systems is just expensive, especially as a student. I already owned Sony lenses, and once you have a collection of lenses, changing camera systems means potentially having to replace a lot more than just the camera body.

Still, getting to try the Nikon Z5II was a really interesting experience. At the time, I was shooting with the Sony A6700, which has a really compact and portable body. The Z5II felt noticeably bigger in comparison, especially being a full-frame camera. You could feel the difference as soon as you picked it up. I spent a good amount of time just getting familiar with ittrying out the dials, buttons, menus, and featuresand honestly, I really liked the camera. It was one of those experiences where you start thinking, okay, maybe I could actually see myself using this.
I even considered switching to Nikon for a moment, but, well... my student budget had other plans.

That said, I do have this weird little bucket-list idea of eventually owning a camera from different manufacturers. I want to try Fuji, Olympus, Nikon, Canon, and, of course, I already have Sony. Why I originally went with Sony is a story for another shoot, though.

For the photographs themselves, I decided to split the day into three different posts on Instagram because each set represented something different about the way I photograph. Clean Studio The first set was the clean studio portraits . Up until this point, most of the photography I had been posting leaned toward creative or abstract work. I hadn't really done a proper clean studio portrait session where the goal was simply to make a polished, straightforward portrait.

The white background, soft lighting, and simple styling gave me a chance to focus more on the subject, pose, and composition without needing a complicated environment. I actually liked having that restraint. It was a nice reminder that I don't always need something abstract happening in the frame to make an image work. Image: clean-portrait-nikon_shoot-5 Editorial title: Quiet Confidence Image description: A clean studio fashion portrait against a bright white seamless background. The subject leans casually against a stool, creating a relaxed editorial pose with plenty of negative space around her. Story connection: Represents the first side of the shootthe clean, straightforward studio portraiture that was different from the user's predominantly creative and abstract work at the time. Monotone The second set was much more familiar territory for me: moody monotone portraits I really like working with monochrome because removing color changes what you pay attention to. Instead of thinking about saturation and the relationship between different colors, I start noticing the lighting, shapes, textures, expression, and overall structure of the photograph.

This set had a much darker and more introspective feeling, which is closer to the kind of visual language I naturally gravitate toward. Image: moody-portrait-nikon_shoot-7 Editorial title: Inward Image description: A dramatic monochrome portrait against a completely dark background. The subject looks downward with her hands held near her chest, creating an introspective and cinematic atmosphere. Story connection: Represents the visual language the user was already naturally drawn towardthe use of monochrome to emphasize lighting, composition, texture, and emotion instead of color. Shutter Drag And then there was the third set, which was probably the most me of the three: shutter drag I'd only recently learned how to use shutter drag, and I thought it would be fun to experiment with it toward the end of the shoot. Instead of trying to get a perfectly sharp portrait, the slower shutter allowed movement to become part of the photograph.

The subject's hands and head created these strange trails and distortions, almost turning the portrait into something more abstract and psychological. I really enjoyed seeing how different the result felt from a normal portrait. The motion wasn't something I was trying to fixit was the photograph. Once I saw how it was coming together, I knew I wanted to make the shutter-drag images their own post. Image: drag-portrait-nikon_shoot-13 Editorial title: Motion Within Image description: An experimental portrait created through intentional shutter drag. The subject's movement creates trails and distortions around the head and hands while the darker background isolates the motion. Story connection: Represents the most experimental part of the shoot and the user's recent discovery of shutter drag as a creative technique.
